name: swift
description: Curated Swift coding-standards pack for the paragraph advisor. Statements are paraphrased summaries; follow the citations for the authoritative text.

rules.title: Keep each type focused on one responsibility
rules.statement: A type that accumulates dozens of methods and nested members is doing several jobs at once. Split it along its natural seams — parsing, persistence, formatting, coordination — so each piece can be named, understood, and changed independently.
rules.rationale: Small, single-purpose types localize change: a bug fix in one concern cannot silently break another, and each piece can be tested in isolation.

rules.title: Break up god objects
rules.statement: A node that half the graph touches is a god object: every feature routes through it, so every change risks every feature. Carve it into narrower services with explicit interfaces and let callers depend only on the slice they use.
rules.rationale: God objects concentrate coupling and merge conflicts; extracting focused collaborators shrinks the blast radius of any change.

citations.title: Introducing MVVM into your SwiftUI project

rules.title: Keep view models lean
rules.statement: A view model should translate between a view and the domain, not absorb the domain. When one view model grows past a screenful of methods, move business rules into services and models, leaving the view model with presentation state and user-intent handling only.
rules.rationale: Lean view models keep the presentation layer testable and stop the 'massive view controller' problem from reappearing under a new name.

citations.title: Different flavors of view models in Swift

rules.title: Route view actions through the view model
rules.statement: Views should express user intent to their view model, never call services directly. A view that talks straight to a network or persistence service bypasses the layer that exists to make that interaction observable and testable.
rules.rationale: When every side effect flows through the view model, previews and tests can substitute fakes at one seam instead of stubbing services inside view code.

citations.title: Introducing MVVM into your SwiftUI project

rules.title: Point dependencies down the layer stack
rules.statement: Dependencies must flow in one direction: views depend on view models, view models on services, services on models. A model that imports SwiftUI or a service that reaches into a view inverts the stack and welds the domain to the UI framework.
rules.rationale: One-way layering keeps lower layers reusable and compilable without the UI, and makes the dependency graph predictable for anyone reading the code.

rules.title: Inject dependencies instead of reaching for singletons
rules.statement: A `.shared` instance referenced from many call sites is a hidden global: its consumers cannot be tested without it and its lifetime is invisible. Pass dependencies in through initializers (or an environment/dependency container) so each consumer states what it needs.
rules.rationale: Injection makes dependencies explicit and swappable, which is what unit tests, previews, and feature isolation all require.

rules.title: Do not ship force operations (try!, as!)
rules.statement: Every `try!` and `as!` is a crash waiting for the input you did not anticipate. Convert failures into thrown errors, optional casts with graceful fallbacks, or precondition checks with explicit messages — reserve force forms for provably-safe cases like compiled-in resources.
rules.rationale: Forced operations turn recoverable conditions into production crashes and hide the failure path from the type system.

citations.title: Error Handling — The Swift Programming Language

rules.title: Use @MainActor instead of DispatchQueue.main in observable types
rules.statement: Observable state that drives SwiftUI must mutate on the main actor, and hopping there with `DispatchQueue.main.async` is unchecked by the compiler. Annotate the type (or its UI-facing members) with `@MainActor` so isolation is verified at compile time and the manual hops disappear.
rules.rationale: @MainActor turns a runtime threading convention into a compiler guarantee, eliminating a whole class of data races on UI state.

citations.title: Protect mutable state with Swift actors (WWDC21)

rules.title: Protect shared mutable state with actors
rules.statement: When several tasks read and write the same state, wrap that state in an actor rather than guarding it with locks or serial queues. The actor serializes access for you and the compiler rejects unsynchronized touches from outside.
rules.rationale: Actors move data-race prevention from convention to the type system, which locks and queues cannot do.

citations.title: Protect mutable state with Swift actors (WWDC21)

rules.title: Prefer structs and value semantics by default
rules.statement: Reach for a struct first and use a class only when identity, shared mutable state, or Objective-C interop genuinely requires it. Value types copy on assignment, so distant code cannot mutate your data behind your back.
rules.rationale: Value semantics remove aliasing bugs and make data safe to pass across concurrency domains.

citations.title: Structures and Classes — The Swift Programming Language

rules.title: Name APIs for clarity at the point of use
rules.statement: Design names so the call site reads as a sentence: include the words needed to avoid ambiguity, omit the ones that merely repeat type information. Judge every signature by how it looks where it is called, not where it is declared.
rules.rationale: Code is read at call sites far more often than at declarations; clear use-site grammar prevents misuse without documentation.
rules.snippet_good:
func remove(_ element: Element, at index: Int) { }

list.remove(item, at: 3)   // reads as a sentence

rules.title: Name methods to reflect side effects and mutation
rules.statement: Use imperative verbs for mutating operations and noun or participle forms for their non-mutating counterparts — `sort()` mutates in place while `sorted()` returns a copy. The name alone should tell a reader whether the receiver changes.
rules.rationale: Consistent mutating/non-mutating pairs let readers reason about state changes without opening the implementation.
rules.snippet_good:
var scores = [3, 1, 2]
scores.sort()              // imperative verb: mutates in place
let ranked = scores.sorted() // participle: returns a new value

rules.title: Abstract collaborators behind protocols for testability
rules.statement: Depend on a small protocol that describes the capability you need, not on the concrete type that happens to provide it. Tests and previews then supply lightweight conformances instead of spinning up real networking or persistence.
rules.rationale: Protocol seams are the cheapest way to make Swift code testable, and they keep call sites honest about which capabilities they actually use.

rules.title: Prefer the @Observable macro for new state models
rules.statement: For projects targeting iOS 17/macOS 14 and later, use the `@Observable` macro instead of `ObservableObject` with `@Published`. Observation tracks exactly which properties a view reads, so views re-render only when those properties change.
rules.rationale: Per-property tracking removes the over-invalidation that objectWillChange causes and deletes the @Published boilerplate.

citations.title: Migrating from the Observable Object protocol to the Observable macro

rules.title: Keep SwiftData models at the model layer
rules.statement: `@Model` classes are persistence entities; keep queries, predicates, and model-context work behind a repository or service instead of scattering them through views. Views should receive plain data or observed models, not compose fetch descriptors inline.
rules.rationale: Containing SwiftData behind one boundary keeps the schema evolvable and lets the rest of the app be tested without a model container.

rules.title: Model recoverable failures explicitly
rules.statement: Give failure paths first-class types: throw domain-specific errors or return `Result` values instead of returning nil, logging, and carrying on. A caller that can see which failures are possible can decide which ones to recover from.
rules.rationale: Explicit error types turn silent degradation into handled cases and make failure behavior part of the reviewed API surface.
